title: Living ashtpadi 22
tomorrow: Ashtpadi 23, salok: the ointment of wisdom

segments.voice: Yesterday, rijak, and your line: he feeds all. A week ends today. It began before creation, he alone was; then the play began, the quiet behind all things, the Lord of all, every heart, and the One who feeds every creature. Today we live it. Day five hundred twenty-five.

Sikhs tell a story about the seventh Guru, Guru Har Rai, when he was a boy. Walking through a garden in a long, flowing robe, he brushed past a flowering bush, and a few petals fell to the ground. His grandfather, Guru Hargobind, saw it and told him gently that a robe that wide must be carried with care. The boy, the story goes, was so moved that he kept that care all his life. Today the twenty-second ashtpadi steps out into the garden.
screen: `A BOY, A ROBE, A FLOWERING BUSH.` → `A FEW PETALS FALL.` → `CARRY IT WITH CARE.`

segments.voice: Here's the twenty-second ashtpadi in brief. God is the thaakur, the Master, of jeea jant, every living being. The One is spread through them all, dwelling ghat ghat, in every heart, and sustaining each creature with its daily bread. Put that together and you get one plain line: everything alive is His. Living it starts with how we touch things. The story of Guru Har Rai is a story people tell, passed down in Sikh tradition rather than recorded in the Guru Granth Sahib. But its point fits the ashtpadi exactly. If every living thing belongs to the One, then a flower isn't just scenery and an animal isn't just a resource. They're in someone else's care, and we're walking through the garden. Sikh tradition remembers Guru Har Rai as a lover of gardens and animals, and as someone who kept medicines to give to the sick, including, by many accounts, the son of the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan, whose family were no friends of the Gurus. That detail matters. Everything alive is His, including the people we'd rather not help. In practice, this can be very small. Watering the office plant that everyone forgets. Driving a little slower past the park. Asking how the elderly neighbor's dog is doing. None of it is grand. But each small act says: this life isn't mine to waste. It belongs to the One who is spread through all.
screen: `THE ASHTPADI: MASTER, PRESENT, FEEDER.` · `A STORY PEOPLE TELL.` · `MEDICINE FOR AN ENEMY'S SON.` · `SMALL ACTS OF CARE.` · then, large: `EVERYTHING ALIVE IS HIS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: care for one living thing. Yesterday was food; today is care. Choose one: a plant that needs water, a bit of litter on the path outside, a tired person in your home who needs a cup of tea. Do it slowly, as if it belonged to someone you love, because in the ashtpadi's picture it does. If there's nothing nearby, sit and picture a living thing you'll care for later today, and plan exactly how. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you tend it. The bell holds the time.
Jeea, living beings, those with life and breath: every jeea has the same Master, the same indwelling Light, the same Feeder; so every living thing is handled with care.
Your line: everything alive is his. Today, find one neglected living thing, a plant, an animal, a person, and give it a moment of real care. Day five hundred twenty-five.

trapdoor: what you thought: everything alive is his is a nice thought about nature.
what it means: every life is in God's care, so we handle plants, animals and people, even enemies, with care.
what a scholar hears: Sikh tradition credits Guru Har Rai with gardens and a dispensary at Kiratpur, and many accounts say he sent medicine for Shah Jahan's son, Dara Shikoh.
